claim: Metagenomic sequencing from apple rootstock rhizospheres resulted in approximately 2 billion quality reads at 150 bp length after filtration.
source: Metagenomic sequencing obtained from the rhizosphere of apple rootstocks grown in orchard soil with a documented history of replant disease resulted in a total of approximately 2 billion quality reads (after filtration) at a length of 150 bp, as described in Berihu et al., 2023.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the sequencing output and references the source study (Berihu et al., 2023).

claim: Independent metagenomics assemblies of six different treatments yielded 1.4–2 million contigs longer than 2 kbp.
source: Independent metagenomics assemblies of six different treatments yielded 1.4–2 million contigs longer than 2 kbp (Berihu et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific quantitative data about contig assembly results with citation to the source.

claim: Binning using MetaWRAP produced 296–433 high-quality MAGs for each of the six treatments.
source: Here, assemblies were binned using MetaWRAP (Uritskiy et al., 2018) into 296–433 high-quality MAGs for each of the six treatments (Figure 2—source data 1); completion and contamination thresholds were set to 90/5, respectively (Bowers et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of MAGs obtained per treatment with specific quality thresholds and citations.

claim: De-replication of 2233 MAGs at 99% average nucleotide identity yielded 395 unique MAGs.
source: De-replication (the process of combining highly similar genomes into a single representative genome) requiring 99% average nucleotide identity of the overall 2233 MAGs yielded a collection of 395 unique MAGs (Figure 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers for the de-replication process and references Figure 2.

claim: 30–36% of raw reads across samples were mapped to the MAG collection.
source: Across samples, 30–36% of the raw reads were mapped to the MAG collection (Figure 2—source data 2), in comparison to 61–71% mapped to the non-binned contigs (Berihu et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages of read mapping with comparison to non-binned contigs.

claim: Taxonomic annotations were assigned at the phylum level for 395 MAGs, order level for 394 MAGs, genus level for 237 MAGs, and species level for 3 MAGs.
source: Using GTDB-Tk (Chaumeil et al., 2019), taxonomic annotations were assigned at the phylum, order, genus, and species level for 395, 394, 237, and three of the de-replicated MAGs, respectively, reflecting the genuine diversity of the rhizosphere community, which include many uncharacterized species (Buée et al., 2009).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of MAGs annotated at each taxonomic level with citations.

claim: Proteobacteria, Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes were identified as the dominant phyla in the apple rhizosphere.
source: As in previous reports (Zhalnina et al., 2018; Xu et al., 2018), Proteobacteria, Acidobacteria, Actinobacteria, and Bacteroidetes were identified as the dominant phyla in the apple rhizosphere (Figure 2A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies dominant phyla with citations to previous reports and reference to Figure 2A.

claim: MAGs were classified into 143 genera compared to approximately 3000 genera identified using gene-centric approaches and approximately 1000 genera based on amplicon sequencing.
source: At the genus level, MAGs were classified into 143 genera in comparison to approximately 3000 genera that were identified for the same data based on gene-centric approaches (Berihu et al., 2023) and approximately 1000 genera based on amplicon sequencing (Somera et al., 2021) of the same data.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numbers comparing different taxonomic classification approaches with citations.

claim: The 10 most frequent functional categories across the MAG collection were involved in primary metabolism.
source: The 10 most frequent functional categories across the MAG collection were involved in primary metabolism, for example, carbohydrate metabolism, and the biosynthesis of essential cellular building blocks such as amino acids and vitamins.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the functional categories identified in the MAG collection.

claim: The prevalence of amino acid biosynthetic pathways across MAGs ranges from 99.5% for glycine to 21% for tyrosine.
source: The prevalence of biosynthetic pathways across MAGs (requiring at least a single relevant enzyme) ranges from 99.5% (e.g., glycine; missing in only two genomes) to 21% (e.g., tyrosine; detected in only 83 MAGs).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages for pathway prevalence with examples.

claim: The majority of bacterial soil species rely on an external supply of at least some of their obligatory nutritional demands.
source: Notably, the diversity of metabolic pathway completeness regarding amino acids and other essential cellular components suggests that the majority of bacterial soil species rely on an external supply of at least some of their obligatory nutritional demands.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion based on pathway completeness analysis.

claim: A set of 395 GSMMs was constructed for the entire collection of rhizosphere-bacterial community MAGs.
source: To better understand environment-dependent metabolic activity occurring in a native rhizosphere, a set of 395 GSMMs was constructed for the entire collection of the rhizosphere-bacterial community MAGs.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of GSMMs constructed.

claim: 243 GSMMs passed stoichiometric consistency tests using MEMOTE.
source: All models were systematically subjected to validity and quality tests using MEMOTE (Lieven et al., 2020), leaving a total of 243 GSMMs whose stoichiometric consistency was confirmed (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of GSMMs that passed quality tests with citation.

claim: GSMMs included on average 1924 reactions, 203 exchange reactions, and 1312 metabolites.
source: On average, GSMMs included 1924 reactions, from which 203 were exchange reactions (specific reactions carrying out extracellular import and secretion of metabolites) and 1312 metabolites (Figure 2—source data 5).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific average values for GSMM attributes.

claim: The GSMM set held 5152 unique metabolic reactions, 597 exchange reactions, and 2671 different compounds.
source: Altogether, the GSMM set held 5152 unique metabolic reactions, 597 exchange reactions, and 2671 different compounds.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total unique features across all GSMMs.

claim: The metabolic coverage of the GSMM data is within the same order of magnitude as described in recent large-scale automatic reconstructions.
source: Additionally, comparison of GSMM scales indicated that the metabolic coverage (i.e., the number of reactions, which denote the potential of executing a metabolic function) of our data is within the same order of magnitude as described in recent large-scale automatic reconstructions (Basile et al., 2020; Heinken et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly compares their results to published studies with citations.

claim: Growth performances were higher on poor medium supplemented with exudates compared to poor medium alone but lower than growth in rich medium.
source: As expected, growth performances were higher on the poor medium supplemented with exudates in comparison to growth on the poor medium alone but lower than the growth in rich medium (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the growth comparison across media types with reference to Figure 3.

claim: GSMM growth patterns were not phylogenetically conserved and were inconsistent between related taxa.
source: Notably, GSMM growth patterns were not phylogenetically conserved and were inconsistent between related taxa.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this observation about growth patterns.

claim: The effect of exudates on community members is selective and differs between species.
source: This inconsistency indicates that the effect of exudates on community members is selective and differs between species (i.e., exudates increase the growth rates of some species more than others), as was previously reported (Zhalnina et al., 2018; Sasse et al., 2018; Stringlis et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this conclusion with citations to supporting literature.

claim: The rhizosphere environment was composed of 60 inorganic compounds together with 33 root exudates.
source: Overall, the rhizosphere environment was composed of 60 inorganic compounds together with the 33 root exudates (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the composition of the simulated environment.

claim: Application of MCSM over the rhizosphere environment supported the growth of 27 GSMMs in the first iteration.
source: Application of MCSM over the 'rhizosphere environment' (i.e., first iteration, root exudates, and 'inorganic compounds', Figure 4—source data 1) supported the growth of 27 GSMMs (Figures 3 and 4B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of GSMMs that grew in the first iteration.

claim: The initial environment was updated with 145 additional compounds predicted to be secreted by growing community members after the first iteration.
source: Then, the initial environment was updated with 145 additional compounds predicted to be secreted by the growing community members.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of compounds added after the first iteration.

claim: The second iteration supported the growth of 33 additional species.
source: The second iteration supported the growth of 33 additional species whose growth was supported by compounds predicted to be secreted by bacteria that grew in the first iteration.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of additional species that grew in the second iteration.

claim: The third iteration supported the growth of 11 additional GSMMs.
source: The third iteration supported the growth of 11 additional GSMMs, with one additional compound secreted.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of GSMMs that grew in the third iteration.

claim: Iterative growth simulations resulted in the successive growth of 71 species after three iterations.
source: Overall, iterative growth simulations resulted in the successive growth of 71 species (Figure 4B; iterations 1–3).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of species that grew across the first three iterations.

claim: 31 additional organic P compounds were added to the medium at the beginning of the fourth iteration.
source: At the beginning of the fourth iteration, 31 additional organic P compounds were identified by screening the species-specific poor medium and were added to the medium (Figure 4—source data 1; organic phosphorous compounds).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of organic P compounds added in the fourth iteration.

claim: The additional organic P compounds supported the growth of nine additional GSMMs in the fourth iteration.
source: The additional organic P compounds supported the growth of nine additional GSMMs (Figure 4B) and led to the secretion of 13 new compounds, which were added to the environment.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of GSMMs that grew after adding organic P compounds.

claim: The fifth iteration supported the growth of four additional GSMMs.
source: The fifth iteration supported the growth of four additional GSMMs and two new compounds were secreted.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of GSMMs that grew in the fifth iteration.

claim: The successive iterations connected 84 out of 243 native members of the apple rhizosphere GSMM community via trophic exchanges.
source: Overall, the successive iterations connected 84 out of 243 native members of the apple rhizosphere GSMM community via trophic exchanges.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the total number of GSMMs connected through the iterative process.

claim: 27 bacterial species grew on the first iteration representing 14 of the 17 phyla included in the initial model collection.
source: In terms of the phylogenetic distribution of the models, 27 bacterial species grew on the first iteration (in which root exudates served as the sole organic sources). These bacteria represented 14 of the 17 phyla included in the initial model collection (consisting of 243 GSMMs) and maintained a distribution frequency similar to the original community.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the phylogenetic representation of first iteration growers.

claim: Most species which grew in the first iteration belonged to the phyla Acidobacteriota, Proteobacteria, and Bacteroidota.
source: As in the full GSMM dataset (Community bar, Figure 4C), most of the species which grew in the first iteration belonged to the phyla Acidobacteriota, Proteobacteria, and Bacteroidota.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies the dominant phyla in the first iteration.

claim: Bacteria assigned to Acidobacteriota, Proteobacteria, and Bacteroidota are the primary beneficiaries of root exudates.
source: This result concurred with findings from the work of Zhalnina et al., which reported that bacteria assigned to these phyla are the primary beneficiaries of root exudates (Zhalnina et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with citation to supporting literature.

claim: Species from Elusimicrobiota, Chlamydiota, and Fibrobacterota phyla did not grow in the first iteration but grew on the second iteration.
source: Species from 3 out of the 17 phyla that did not grow in the first iteration – Elusimicrobiota, Chlamydiota, and Fibrobacterota, did grow on the second iteration (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies phyla that grew in the second but not first iteration.

claim: Members of the Elusimicrobiota phylum include mostly uncultured species whose nutritional preferences are likely to be selective.
source: Members of these phyla are known for their specialized metabolic dependencies. Such is the case for example with members of the Elusimicrobiota phylum, which include mostly uncultured species whose nutritional preferences are likely to be selective (Uzun et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this characteristic of Elusimicrobiota with citation.

claim: Bacteria classified as Sphingomonadales grew in the initial root environment.
source: At the order level, bacteria classified as Sphingomonadales (class Alphaproteobacteria), a group known to include typical inhabitants of the root environment (Lei et al., 2019), grew in the initial root environment.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states which order grew in the first iteration with citation.

claim: Rhizobiales and Burkholderiales did not grow in the first iteration but grew in the second and third iterations, respectively.
source: In comparison, other root-inhabiting groups including the orders Rhizobiales and Burkholderiales (Lei et al., 2019), did not grow in the first iteration. Rhizobiales and Burkholderiales did, however, grow in the second and third iterations, respectively, indicating that in the simulations, the growth of these groups was dependent on exchange metabolites secreted by other community members (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states when these orders grew and infers their metabolic dependencies.

claim: 158 organic compounds were secreted throughout the MCSM simulation, of which 12 compounds overlapped with the original exudate medium.
source: Overall, 158 organic compounds were secreted throughout the MCSM simulation (from which 12 compounds overlapped with the original exudate medium).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of secreted compounds and overlap with exudates.

claim: Microbial-secreted compounds included siderophores, vitamins, and coenzymes.
source: Microbial-secreted compounds included siderophores (staphyloferrin, salmochelin, pyoverdine, and enterochelin), vitamins (pyridoxine, pantothenate, and thiamin), and coenzymes (coenzyme A, flavin adenine dinucleotide, and flavin mononucleotide) – all known to be exchange compounds in microbial communities (Ghosh et al., 2017; Lu et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists specific compounds secreted by microbes with citations.

claim: Microbial secretions included 11 amino acids.
source: In addition, microbial secretions included 11 amino acids (arginine, lysine, threonine, alanine, serine, phenylalanine, tyrosine, leucine, glutamate, isoleucine, and methionine), also known as a common exchange currency in microbial communities (Mee et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly lists the amino acids secreted with citation.

claim: The community-exchange network was constructed as a directed bipartite graph with 84 GSMM nodes and 203 metabolite nodes connected by 9773 directed edges.
source: The network was built as a directed bipartite graph, in which the 84 feasible GSMM nodes and the 203 metabolite nodes (27 root exudates, 146 microbial-secreted compounds, and 30 additional organic-P compounds) were connected by 9773 directed edges, representing the metabolic exchanges of organic compounds in the native apple rhizosphere community (Figure 5A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the network structure with specific numbers.

claim: The network included 45,972 unique PM paths and 571,605 unique PMM paths.
source: Overall, the network included 45,972 unique PM paths and 571,605 unique PMM paths.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of each type of path in the network.

claim: Participation of GSMMs in PM paths ranged from 272 to 896 occurrences.
source: Participation of GSMMs in PM paths ranged from 272 to 896 occurrences (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the range of GSMM participation in PM paths.

claim: GSMM participation in PMM paths ranged from 398 to 50,628 in the first microbe position and 1388–19,738 occurrences in the second microbe position.
source: GSSM participation in PMM paths ranged from 398 to 50,628 in the first microbe position (primary exudate consumer) and 1388–19,738 occurrences in the second microbe position (secondary consumer) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B, C).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the range of GSMM participation in PMM paths at different positions.

claim: Frequency of GSMMs in the first position in PMM sub-network motifs was negatively correlated with the frequency of presence in second positions (Pearson = −0.279; p-value = 0.009).
source: Frequency of GSMMs in the first position in PMM sub-network motifs was negatively correlated with the frequency of presence in second positions, possibly indicating species-specific preferences for a specific position/trophic level in the defined environment (Pearson = −0.279; p-value = 0.009, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the correlation with statistical values and infers biological meaning.

claim: GSMMs classified as S initiated a significantly higher number of PMM sub-networks than GSMMs classified as NA and H.
source: GSMMs classified as S initiated a significantly higher number of PMM sub-networks (located in the first position) than GSMMs classified as NA and H (Figure 6A).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this significant difference with reference to Figure 6A.

claim: Non-beneficial bacteria may have a broader spectrum in terms of their utilization potential of root-secreted carbon sources compared to plant-beneficial bacteria.
source: The higher number of trophic interactions formed by the S-classified primary exudate consumers in the PMM sub-network motifs suggests that non-beneficial bacteria may have a broader spectrum in terms of their utilization potential of root-secreted carbon sources compared to plant-beneficial bacteria.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this interpretation based on the network analysis.

claim: Three root exudates were found to be significantly more prevalent in H-classified PM paths.
source: Considering consumed metabolites (root exudates), three and six compounds were found to be significantly more prevalent in H- and S-classified PM paths, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of exudates associated with healthy paths.

claim: Six root exudates were found to be significantly more prevalent in S-classified PM paths.
source: Considering consumed metabolites (root exudates), three and six compounds were found to be significantly more prevalent in H- and S-classified PM paths, respectively (Figure 6B).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of exudates associated with sick paths.

claim: S-classified root exudates included gallic acid and caffeic acid, which are phenylpropanoids secreted from plant roots following exposure to replant pathogens.
source: Notably, the S-classified root exudates included compounds reported to support dysbiosis and ARD progression. For example, the S-classified compounds gallic acid and caffeic acid (3,4-dihidroxy-trans-cinnamate) are phenylpropanoids – phenylalanine intermediate phenolic compounds secreted from plant roots following exposure to replant pathogens (Balbín-Suárez et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies specific compounds and their characteristics with citation.

claim: High levels of phenolic compounds can have autotoxic effects, potentially exacerbating ARD.
source: Though secretion of these compounds is considered a defense response, it is hypothesized that high levels of phenolic compounds can have autotoxic effects, potentially exacerbating ARD.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this hypothesis about phenolic compounds.

claim: Genes associated with the production of caffeic acid were upregulated in ARD-infected apple roots relative to those grown in γ-irradiated ARD soil.
source: Additionally, it was shown that genes associated with the production of caffeic acid were upregulated in ARD-infected apple roots, relative to those grown in γ-irradiated ARD soil (Weiß et al., 2017b; Weiß et al., 2017a), and that root and soil extracts from replant-diseased trees inhibited apple seedling growth and resulted in increased seedling root production of caffeic acid (Sun et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding with citations to supporting studies.

claim: A total of 79 unique compounds were found to be significantly overrepresented in either S (42 compounds) or H (41 compounds) classified PM paths.
source: As to the microbial-secreted compounds, a total of 79 unique compounds were found to be significantly overrepresented in either S (42 compounds) or H (41 compounds) classified PM paths (Figure 6C, D).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of compounds associated with each classification.

claim: L-sorbose and phenylacetaladehyde were over-represented in H paths and have been shown to inhibit the growth of fungal pathogens associated with replant disease.
source: For instance, the compounds L-sorbose (EX_srb__L_e) and phenylacetaladehyde (EX_pacald_e), both over-represented in H paths (Figure 6C), have been shown to inhibit the growth of fungal pathogens associated with replant disease (Howell, 1978; Zou et al., 2007).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly identifies these compounds and their functions with citations.

claim: Phenylacetaladehyde has nematicidal qualities.
source: Phenylacetaladehyde has also been reported to have nematicidal qualities (Gomes et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this property with citation.

claim: The root exudate 4-hydroxybenzoate is metabolized by GSMM_091 (class Verrucomicrobiae, order Pedosphaerales) to catechol.
source: The root exudate 4-hydroxybenzoate is metabolized by GSMM_091 (class Verrucomicrobiae, order Pedosphaerales) to catechol.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this metabolic pathway.

claim: Catechol is a precursor of catecholamines, which were shown to increase apple tolerance to ARD symptoms when added to orchard.
source: Catechol is a precursor of a number of catecholamines, a group of compounds which was recently shown to increase apple tolerance to ARD symptoms when added to orchard (Berihu et al., 2023; Gao et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this relationship with citations.

claim: 4-hydroxybenzoate can serve as a selective enhancer of catecholamine synthesizing bacteria associated with reduced ARD symptoms.
source: This analysis (PM; Figure 5C) leads to formulating the testable prediction that 4-hydroxybenzoate can serve as a selective enhancer of catecholamine synthesizing bacteria associated with reduced ARD symptoms, and therefore serve as a potential source for indigenously produced beneficial compounds.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly formulates this prediction based on the analysis.

claim: The framework combines metagenomics analyses with constraint-based modeling to understand rhizosphere bacterial functionality.
source: In this study, we present a framework combining metagenomics analyses with CBM, which can be used to gain a deeper understanding of the functionality, dynamics, and division of labor among rhizosphere bacteria, and link their environment-dependent metabolism to biological significance.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the framework approach.

claim: GSMMs were constructed using CarveMe, a python-based tool for GSMM reconstruction.
source: GSMMs were constructed for each of the 395 MAGs using CarveMe v 1.5.1 (Machado et al., 2018,) a python-based tool for GSMM reconstruction.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the tool used for GSMM construction with citation.

claim: All GSMMs were drafted without gap filling as it might mask metabolic co-dependencies.
source: All GSMMs were drafted without gap filling as it might mask metabolic co-dependencies (Opatovsky et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this methodological choice with citation and rationale.

claim: MCSM uses FVA to determine exchange fluxes rather than FBA.
source: Unlike FBA, which is used for gathering an arbitrary solution regarding non-optimized fluxes, the MCSM uses FVA to determine exchange fluxes (Mahadevan and Schilling, 2003).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the methodological approach with citation.

claim: The FVA fraction of optimum was set to 0.9, sustaining the objective function at 90% optimality.
source: The FVA fraction of optimum was set to 0.9 (sustaining the objective function at 90% optimality, allowing a less restricted secretion profile).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this parameter setting with rationale.

claim: Metabolomics data from Geneva 935 or Malling 26 rootstock cultivars were used to specify an array of apple root-derived compounds.
source: To this end, metabolomics data from a set of studies which characterized the root exudates of Geneva 935 (G935) or Malling 26 (M26) rootstock cultivars (Leisso et al., 2017; Leisso et al., 2018) – related to the G210 and M26 rootstocks whose rhizobiome was characterized here, were used to specify an array of apple root-derived compounds (Table 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the source of metabolomics data with citations.

claim: The list of secreted compounds was consistent with other reported profiles of plant root exudates.
source: The list of secreted compounds was consistent with other reported profiles of plant root exudates (Zhalnina et al., 2018; Naveed et al., 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this consistency with citations.

claim: The rhizosphere serves as a hotspot for a diversity of interactions spanning from the secretion of organic compounds by plant roots to their uptake by the adjacent soil microbial community.
source: The rhizosphere serves as a hotspot for a diversity of interactions spanning from the secretion of organic compounds by plant roots to their uptake by the adjacent soil microbial community (Zhalnina et al., 2018; Gomariz et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this characteristic of the rhizosphere with citations.

claim: These interactions form a complex network of metabolic exchanges whose structure and function has a considerable impact on plant health.
source: These interactions form a complex network of metabolic exchanges whose structure and function has a considerable impact on plant health (Singh et al., 2004).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this relationship with citation.

claim: Targeted secretion of exudates from plant roots into the environment is fundamental to the recruitment of specific microbes and the assembly of a plant-selected community.
source: Targeted secretion of exudates from plant roots' into the environment is fundamental to the recruitment of specific microbes and the assembly of a plant-selected community (i.e., the rhizobiome) (Korenblum et al., 2020; Sasse et al., 2018; Venturi and Keel, 2016).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this mechanism with citations.

claim: Each plant has a unique profile of exudates guiding the formation of a specialized rhizobiome.
source: Each plant has a unique profile of exudates guiding the formation of a specialized rhizobiome that is adapted to support its mineral absorption (Olanrewaju et al., 2017; Rawat et al., 2021; Compant et al., 2010), secrete plant growth supporting compounds (Finkel et al., 2020; Ghosh et al., 2020; Kudoyarova et al., 2019), and provide protection against soil-borne microorganisms that are detrimental to its health (Berendsen et al., 2012; Ngalimat et al., 2021; Mazzola and Freilich, 2017).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this characteristic with multiple citations.

claim: Constraint-based modeling is an approach that allows for the simulation of bacterial-metabolic activity in a given environment based on the constraints imposed by the annotated microbial genomes.
source: Constraint-based modeling (CBM) is an approach that allows for the simulation of bacterial-metabolic activity in a given environment based on the constraints imposed by the annotated microbial genomes (Faust and Raes, 2012; Orth et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines CBM with citations.

claim: Applying CBM over a GSMM can be used to assess the uptake and secretion of metabolites in the environment under study.
source: Applying CBM over a GSMM can be used to assess the uptake and secretion of metabolites in the environment under study (Orth et al., 2010).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this application with citation.

claim: Advancement of sequencing technologies alongside the development of automatic pipelines for GSMM construction has promoted an increased use of CBM for the modeling of communities with growing complexity.
source: Advancement of sequencing technologies alongside the development of automatic pipelines for GSMM construction (Machado et al., 2018; Henry et al., 2010) has promoted an increased use of CBM for the modeling of communities with growing complexity (Faust and Raes, 2012; Widder et al., 2016; Magnúsdóttir et al., 2017; Basile et al., 2020; Zampieri et al., 2023; Heinken et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this trend with multiple citations.

claim: The relevance of CBM to the study of microbiomes has been demonstrated in a variety of ecosystems.
source: The relevance of CBM to the study of microbiomes has been demonstrated in a variety of ecosystems and recent works have shown that CBM-based predictions can guide the development of strategies for microbiome management (Heinken et al., 2023; Faust, 2019; Xu et al., 2019; Ruan et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this with citations to supporting literature.

claim: Most studies attempting to model the microbiome of specific ecosystems by GSMM represent native species using corresponding genome sequences from public depositories, a process referred to as 16S-based genome imputation.
source: To date, most studies attempting to model the microbiome of specific ecosystems by GSMM represent native species using corresponding genome sequences from public depositories, a process which is usually referred to as 16S-based genome imputation (Basile et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2019; Dhakar et al., 2022).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this common approach with citations.

claim: Genome recovery allows one to obtain full genomes directly from metagenomes.
source: Genome recovery, or genome-resolved metagenomes, often referred to as metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) allows one to obtain full genomes directly from metagenomes (Taş et al., 2021; Uritskiy et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines MAGs with citations.

claim: Constructing GSMMs based on MAGs derived from a specific biological sample enables a genuine view of the metabolic activities carried out in situ.
source: Constructing GSMMs based on MAGs derived from a specific biological sample or directly from a native community enables a genuine view of the metabolic activities carried out in situ, hence bypasses the need in 16S-based genome imputation.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this advantage of using MAGs.

claim: 395 unique MAGs were recovered from metagenomes constructed for the native rhizosphere community of apple rootstocks cultivated in orchard soil affected by apple replant disease.
source: The current study describes the recovery of 395 unique MAGs from metagenomes constructed for the native rhizosphere community of apple rootstocks cultivated in orchard soil affected by apple replant disease (ARD) (Somera et al., 2021; Berihu et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of MAGs recovered with citations.

claim: Soils were amended with Brassicaceae seed meal or were not amended, supporting the development of either disease-suppressive or disease-conducive root microbiomes, respectively.
source: Soils were amended with Brassicaceae seed meal, or were not amended, supporting the development of either disease-suppressive or disease-conducive root microbiomes, respectively (Somera et al., 2021; Berihu et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design with citations.

claim: The framework provides a means for capturing trophic interactions and formulating testable hypotheses regarding the metabolic capabilities of microbial communities within their natural environment.
source: This framework provides a means for capturing trophic interactions and formulating a range of testable hypotheses regarding the metabolic capabilities of microbial communities within their natural environment.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the purpose and utility of the framework.

claim: The framework can be applied to different environments and biological landscapes.
source: Essentially, it can be applied to different environments and biological landscapes, elucidating the conditions for the targeted manipulation of various microbiomes, and the execution of countless predefined functions.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the broad applicability of the framework.

claim: The experimental design included sampling of six different soil/apple rootstock treatments with five biological replicates each.
source: The experimental design included sampling of six different soil/apple rootstock treatments with five biological replicates each, as described in Somera et al., 2021.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the experimental design with citation.

claim: Two different apple rootstocks (M26, ARD susceptible; G210, ARD tolerant) were grown in three different treatments.
source: Two different apple rootstocks (M26, ARD susceptible; G210, ARD tolerant) were grown in three different treatments: (1) orchard soil amended with Brassica napus seed meal, (2) orchard soil amended with Brassica juncea/Sinapis alba seed meal (BjSa), and (3) no-treatment control soil (NTC) (see Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the rootstocks and treatments.

claim: Based on differential abundance, MAGs were classified either as associated with healthy soil (H), sick soil (S), or not-associated with either soil type (NA).
source: Based on DA, MAGs were classified either as associated with healthy soil (H; BjSa DA), sick soil (S; NTC DA), or not-associated with either soil type (NA; not DA at any treatment site).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the classification scheme.

claim: Gene calling and annotation were performed with the Annotate_bins module of MetaWRAP.
source: Gene calling and annotation were performed with the Annotate_bins module of MetaWRAP.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the method used for gene annotation.

claim: Pathway completeness was determined with KEGG Decoder based on the KO annotations.
source: Pathway completeness was determined with KEGG Decoder v 1.0.8.2 (Graham et al., 2018) based on the KO annotations extracted from Annotate_bins assignments.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the method for pathway completeness with citation.

claim: The quality of the genomes was determined with CheckM.
source: The quality of the genomes was determined with CheckM (Parks et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the quality assessment method with citation.

claim: For phylogenomic analyses and taxonomic classification, 120 bacterial marker genes of the MAGs were searched for and aligned using GTDB-Tk.
source: For phylogenomic analyses and taxonomic classification of each bacterial and archaeal genome, we searched for and aligned 120 bacterial marker genes of the MAGs using the identity and align commands of GTDB-Tk v1.5.0 (Chaumeil et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the phylogenomic analysis method with citation.

claim: MAGs were de-replicated using dRep using the default settings.
source: MAGs were de-replicated using dRep v2.3.2 (Olm et al., 2017) using the default settings and MAGs from the six assemblies were clustered into a single non-redundant set.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the de-replication method with citation.

claim: A set of 395 high-quality genomes (≥90% completeness, <5% contamination) was used for downstream analyses.
source: Overall, a set of 395 high-quality genomes (≥90% completeness,<5% contamination) was used for downstream analyses.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the quality thresholds for the final MAG set.

claim: The solver used for GSMM reconstruction is Cplex (v. 12.8.0.0).
source: The solver used for GSMM reconstruction is Cplex (v. 12.8.0.0).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the solver used.

claim: Analyses and simulations of GSMMs were conducted via COBRApy.
source: Analyses and simulations of GSMMs, as well as retrieval of model attributes (reactions, metabolites, exchanges, etc.), were conducted via the vast array of methods found in COBRApy (Ebrahim et al., 2013), a python coding language package for analyzing constraint-based reconstructions.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the software used with citation.

claim: The rich medium was composed of all the exchange reactions a model holds.
source: The rich medium was composed of all the exchange reactions (i.e., exchange reaction for specific compounds) a model holds, gathered by the 'exchanges' attribute found in each model.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the rich medium composition.

claim: The poor medium was composed of the minimal set of compounds required for a specific GSMM/species to grow at a fixed rate.
source: The poor medium was composed of the minimal set of compounds required for a specific GSMM/species to grow at a fixed rate. This set of compounds was identified using the minimal_medium module from COBRApy (minimize components = True, growth rate of 0.1 biomass increase hour−1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly defines the poor medium composition and method.

claim: Exudate compounds were aligned with the BIGG database to format them for use in COBRApy.
source: Exudate compounds were aligned with the BIGG database (King et al., 2016) in order to format them for use in COBRApy.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the formatting process with citation.

claim: GSMM growth rates were calculated by solving each model using the summary method in COBRApy, which utilizes Flux Balance Analysis for maximizing biomass.
source: For each media type, GSMM growth rates were calculated by solving each model using the summary method in COBRApy, which utilizes Flux Balance Analysis (FBA) for maximizing biomass.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the growth rate calculation method.

claim: FVA gathers the full range of exchange fluxes that satisfy the objective function of a GSMM.
source: FVA gathers the full range of exchange fluxes (both secretion and uptake) that satisfy the objective function of a GSMM (i.e., biomass increase).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes what FVA does.

claim: Secretion compounds added to the updated medium in each iteration were set to be given in optimal fluxes in next iteration.
source: Secretion compounds added to the updated medium in each iteration were set to be given in optimal fluxes in next iteration, to ensure a metabolic effect based on the presence of specific metabolites in the environment, rather than their quantity.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes this methodological choice with rationale.

claim: Flux boundaries of updated medium components were set to 1000 mmol/gDW hour.
source: Flux boundaries of updated medium components were set to 1000 mmol/gDW hour (for a specific exchange compound; gDW, gram Dry Weight).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this parameter setting.

claim: Secreted metabolites were classified into biochemical categories based on BRITE annotations or manually in the absence of classification.
source: Along MCSM iterations, secreted metabolites were classified into biochemical categories based on BRITE annotations (Aoki-Kinoshita and Kanehisa, 2007) or, in the absence of classification, manually.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the classification method with citation.

claim: The network was constructed with the networkx package, a python language package for the exploration and analysis of networks and network algorithms.
source: The network was constructed with the networkx package, a python language package for the exploration and analysis of networks and network algorithms.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the software used for network construction.

claim: Network-specific topography was obtained using the Kamada-kawai layout.
source: Network-specific topography was obtained using the Kamada-kawai layout (Hagberg et al., 2008).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the layout algorithm used with citation.

claim: Untangling the exchange network into individual paths was done using the all_shortest_paths function in networkx.
source: Untangling the exchange network into individual paths (i.e., sub-network motifs) was done using the all_shortest_paths function in networkx (Hagberg et al., 2008), applied over the exchanges network.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the method for path extraction with citation.

claim: The distribution of counts of classified sub-networks at different positions was compared using the ANOVA test, followed by a Tukey test.
source: For PMMs, the distribution of counts of classified sub-networks, at the different positions, was compared using the ANOVA test, followed by a Tukey test to significantly distinguish the groups.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the statistical methods used.

claim: Start/end metabolites in PM paths were associated with H/S/NA paths based on one-sided hypergeometric test.
source: On that account, start/end metabolites in PM paths were associated with H/S/NA paths based on one-sided hypergeometric test, comparing the frequency of each compound in a functionally characterized path type (either H or S) vs its frequency in NA classified paths and the reciprocal dataset.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly describes the statistical method for metabolite association.
